summary: Specifies Multipath TCP, a set of extensions that let a single TCP connection use several paths at once. Applications still see an ordinary reliable byte stream, while the network gets better resource use, throughput, and resilience to failure. It obsoletes RFC 6824.

plainLanguage.summary: Multipath TCP lets one connection between two hosts use several network paths at the same time, for example a wired link and a wireless link. The applications still see one ordinary reliable byte stream, while the network gets better use of its capacity and the connection survives the loss of one path.

subtitle: Extensions that let one TCP connection carry its data over several network paths at once.

tldr.problem: A normal TCP connection is pinned to one path between two hosts. If that path is slow or breaks, the connection suffers even though the hosts have other addresses and other routes available.
tldr.mechanism: Multipath TCP adds a TCP option carrying subtypes. The first subflow exchanges 64-bit keys with MP_CAPABLE, later subflows join with MP_JOIN, and every subflow maps its own 32-bit sequence numbers onto a shared 64-bit data sequence number so the receiver can put the bytes back in order.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8684 replaces the experimental RFC 6824 and specifies MPTCP version 1, which is not compatible with version 0. Applications see one ordinary byte stream, and the connection falls back to plain TCP when a middlebox blocks the new options.

facts.label: Token
facts.value: Most significant 32 bits of the SHA-256 hash of the key

facts.label: MP_CAPABLE option length
facts.value: 4 on SYN, 12 on SYN/ACK, 20 on ACK, 22 or 24 with data

facts.value: 0x0 to 0x8, with 0xf reserved for private use

today: RFC 8684 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 6824, which was Experimental, and specifies MPTCP version 1, which is not backward compatible with version 0. The architecture, congestion control and application interface are described separately in RFC 6182, RFC 6356 and RFC 6897.

sections.title: One Connection, Several Paths
sections.content:
Multipath TCP (MPTCP) is a set of extensions to regular TCP that provide a Multipath TCP service, which enables a transport connection to operate across multiple paths simultaneously. This document presents the protocol changes needed to add multipath capability to TCP: signalling and setting up multiple paths, called subflows, managing those subflows, reassembly of data, and termination of sessions.

The design rests on two constraints. It must be backward compatible with current regular TCP, to increase its chances of deployment, and it can be assumed that one or both hosts are multihomed and multiaddressed. To simplify the design, the presence of multiple addresses at a host is taken as sufficient to indicate the existence of multiple paths. Those paths need not be entirely disjoint, since sharing routers does not remove the benefit of better resource utilization and resilience to a subset of node failures.

MPTCP identifies multiple paths by the presence of multiple addresses at the hosts, and it adds connection-level sequence numbers so that segments arriving on subflows with differing network delays can be reassembled. To a program that is not aware of MPTCP, the connection behaves the same as normal TCP, and the extra signalling is handled by the MPTCP implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Multipath TCP lets one connection between two hosts use several network paths at the same time, for example a wired link and a wireless link. The applications still see one ordinary reliable byte stream, while the network gets better use of its capacity and the connection survives the loss of one path.

sections.title: How MPTCP Sits in the Stack
sections.content:
MPTCP operates at the transport layer and aims to be transparent to both higher and lower layers. It is a set of additional features on top of standard TCP, and it is designed to be usable by legacy applications with no changes.

The vocabulary of the document distinguishes a path, which is a sequence of links between a sender and a receiver defined by a 4-tuple of source and destination address and port pairs, from a subflow, which is a flow of TCP segments operating over an individual path and forming part of a larger MPTCP connection. An MPTCP connection is a set of one or more subflows, over which an application can communicate between two hosts, with a one-to-one mapping between a connection and an application socket. The term data-level means connection-level, in contrast to subflow-level, which refers to properties of an individual subflow.

The number of subflows within a connection is not fixed, and it can fluctuate during the lifetime of the connection. All MPTCP operations are signalled with a single TCP option type, with subtypes for each MPTCP message, and each subflow looks to the network layer like a regular TCP flow whose segments carry that new option.
sections.plainLanguage: MPTCP sits where TCP normally sits, between the application and the IP layer. The application opens one socket and sees one stream of bytes. Underneath, MPTCP runs several ordinary TCP connections, one for each path, and joins them into the single stream the application sees.

sections.title: The MPTCP Option and Its Subtypes
sections.content:
All MPTCP operations are signalled using optional TCP header fields. A single TCP option number has been assigned by IANA for MPTCP, and individual messages are determined by a subtype, whose values are also held in an IANA registry. As with all TCP options, the Length field is specified in bytes and includes the 2 bytes of Kind and Length. The subtype is a 4-bit field, the first 4 bits of the option payload.

Subtype 0x0 is MP_CAPABLE, which declares that the sender can perform Multipath TCP and wishes to do so on this connection. Subtype 0x1 is MP_JOIN, which identifies the connection that a new subflow is joining. Subtype 0x2 is DSS, the Data Sequence Signal, which carries the Data Sequence Mapping and a connection-level Data ACK. Subtype 0x3 is ADD_ADDR and 0x4 is REMOVE_ADDR, for telling the peer about another address. Subtype 0x5 is MP_PRIO, for changing a subflow's priority, 0x6 is MP_FAIL for fallback, 0x7 is MP_FASTCLOSE for closing the whole connection, and 0x8 is MP_TCPRST for resetting a single subflow. Values 0x9 through 0xe are unassigned, and 0xf is reserved for private use.

The MP_CAPABLE option starts with Kind and Length, followed by a 4-bit subtype and a 4-bit version field, then a flags octet, then the 64-bit sender's key, then the 64-bit receiver's key, then a 16-bit Data-Level Length and an optional 16-bit checksum. The option length depends on where it appears: 4 bytes on the SYN, 12 on the SYN/ACK, 20 on the ACK, and 22 or 24 on an ACK that carries the first data.
sections.plainLanguage: Every MPTCP message travels in the same new kind of TCP option, and a four-bit code inside it says which message it is. There are nine defined messages, from the handshake to adding a path, and one value is kept for private experiments.

sections.title: Opening a Connection and Adding Paths
sections.content:
Connection initiation begins with a SYN, SYN/ACK and ACK on a single path, each carrying the MP_CAPABLE option. The option verifies that the remote host supports Multipath TCP and lets the hosts exchange information used to authenticate the establishment of additional subflows. Each host generates a random 64-bit key, and the ACK carries both keys, which is the first time the initiator's key appears on the wire and the only time keys are sent in the clear. The token used to identify the connection is a cryptographic hash of the key, truncated to the most significant 32 bits of a SHA-256 hash, while the Initial Data Sequence Number is the least significant 64 bits of that hash.

A new subflow starts as an ordinary TCP SYN/ACK exchange with the MP_JOIN option added. The token identifies which connection the subflow is joining, and a Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) authenticates it. The HMAC uses the keys exchanged in the MP_CAPABLE handshake and the random numbers exchanged in the MP_JOIN options. MP_JOIN also carries flags and an Address ID, which lets a host refer to its own source address without knowing whether a NAT has changed it.

A host may also tell the peer about an address it could use, without opening a subflow on it, using the ADD_ADDR option, which carries an HMAC so that the receiver can tell the address really came from the originator; the receiver echoes the option back to confirm receipt. REMOVE_ADDR withdraws an address by its Address ID. During a connection, MP_PRIO lets one host ask for a change in the priority of a subflow, for example to mark it as a backup path used only when no regular path is available.
sections.plainLanguage: The first path is opened with the usual three-way TCP handshake, and the two hosts exchange a random secret key in it. A later path is opened with an ordinary TCP handshake too, but it carries a token derived from that secret and a keyed hash that proves the two ends share it. A host can also advertise an extra address for the peer to use later.

sections.title: Sending Data and Putting It Back in Order
sections.content:
To ensure reliable, in-order delivery over subflows that may appear and disappear at any time, MPTCP uses a 64-bit Data Sequence Number to number all data sent over the connection. Each subflow keeps its own 32-bit sequence number space, using the regular TCP sequence number header, and an MPTCP option maps the subflow sequence space onto the data sequence space. Data can therefore be retransmitted on a different subflow, mapped to the same Data Sequence Number, if one path fails.

The Data Sequence Signal carries the Data Sequence Mapping, which consists of the subflow sequence number, the data sequence number, and the length for which the mapping is valid. The mapping covers a range of data rather than each packet, which helps when segmentation or coalescing happens outside the stack, and one mapping can cover many packets. A mapping is fixed once declared, although the same data sequence number may be mapped to by different subflows for retransmission.

All subflows share the same receive buffer and advertise the same receive window. There are two levels of acknowledgment: regular TCP acknowledgments on each subflow, and connection-level Data ACKs for the data sequence space, which track the advancement of the byte stream and slide the receive window. When checksums have been negotiated, the mapping also carries a checksum of the data it covers, using the standard TCP checksum over the data with a pseudo-header, so that a middlebox that alters the payload is detected. The checksum algorithm is used to detect whether the payload has been adjusted in any way by a non-MPTCP-aware middlebox.
sections.plainLanguage: Each path keeps its own byte counters, as normal TCP does. On top of that, MPTCP numbers the whole stream of bytes with a single 64-bit counter, and every packet says how the two counters line up. The receiver uses that to put the bytes back in order, no matter which path they arrived on.

sections.title: Closing a Connection and Falling Back
sections.content:
A host that wants to close one subflow but not the whole connection starts a regular TCP FIN and ACK exchange, and a host that has no more data to send signals a connection-level FIN as part of the DSS, which is acknowledged at the connection level with a Data ACK. A regular TCP RST only has the scope of the subflow, so MPTCP adds the MP_FASTCLOSE option for closing the whole connection abruptly. It can be sent on an ACK, which is reliable, or on a RST, which is not. If no TCP RST comes back after one retransmission timeout, the MP_FASTCLOSE SHOULD be retransmitted, with a recommended limit of 3 retransmissions.

Sometimes a middlebox prevents MPTCP from working, most often by removing the new options or by modifying the payload. In that case the protocol falls back: the handshake falls back to regular TCP if either SYN lacks the MPTCP options. If the options get through on the SYN but not on later packets, a sender MUST include a DSS option with a Data Sequence Mapping in every segment until one is acknowledged with a DSS Data ACK. If an ACK for data arrives without such a DSS option, the sender decides the path is not MPTCP capable. On an additional subflow it MUST close that subflow with a RST carrying an MP_TCPRST option with a Middlebox interference reason code; on the first subflow, before any additional subflows are added, the implementation MUST drop out of MPTCP mode and fall back to regular TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Closing one path is an ordinary TCP close. Closing the whole connection needs a new signal, because a normal reset would only close one path. If a device on the path strips the new options, MPTCP notices and quietly goes back to being a plain TCP connection rather than failing.

sections.title: Getting Through Existing Network Equipment
sections.content:
Multipath TCP was designed to be deployable in the present world, and its design takes into account reasonable existing middlebox behaviour. The primary concern is the use of a new TCP option, because some middleboxes strip options, drop packets with new options, copy the same option into multiple segments, or drop options during segment coalescing.

MPTCP uses a single new TCP option and defines all message types as subtype values, which reduces the chance that only some types get through. If an MP_CAPABLE option is dropped on either the outgoing or the return path, the initiating host falls back to regular TCP. If packets carrying MP_JOIN are dropped, the path is simply not used: the SYN then looks like an ordinary SYN, and either the host answers with a SYN/ACK, in which case the initiator sends a RST because the SYN/ACK lacks the token, or the subflow setup fails without affecting the connection as a whole.

If options get through and there is no resegmentation or coalescing, multipath flows proceed without problems. If only some options are stripped, behaviour is not deterministic: the connection can continue so long as mappings exist for the subflow-level data, and if some subflow-level space is left unmapped the subflow is treated as broken and closed. MPTCP is expected to survive a loss of some Data ACKs, but performance degrades as the fraction of stripped options increases.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewalls, NATs and other devices in the path were built before MPTCP existed, and some of them remove unfamiliar TCP options. The protocol is built so that losing those options is not fatal: the connection either works on one path as usual, or it drops one path and carries on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Adding multipath capability to TCP brings new classes of threat, and the fundamental goal is that the security of MPTCP is no worse than that of regular TCP. The key requirements are to confirm that the parties in a subflow handshake are the same as the parties in the original connection setup, to verify that the peer can receive traffic at a new address before using it, and to provide replay protection so that a request to add or remove a subflow is fresh.

MPTCP meets these goals with a hash-based handshake algorithm. The security of the connection hangs on keys that are shared once at the start of the first subflow and are never sent again over the network, except in the Fast Close mechanism. Future subflows use a truncated cryptographic hash of the key, which lets the receiver demultiplex them without revealing cryptographic material. Keys are sent in the clear in the MP_CAPABLE messages, MP_JOIN messages are secured with HMAC-SHA256 using those keys, and standard TCP validity checks are made on the other messages, ensuring that sequence numbers are in-window.

This document also removes the MP_PRIO field that would have let the priority change be applied on a subflow other than the one it was sent on, because it was determined that this could be used by a man-in-the-middle to divert all traffic onto its own path. The ADD_ADDR option now carries an HMAC of the added address, and address advertisements are treated as soft state that an implementation may discard at will.
sections.plainLanguage: Multipath adds ways for an attacker to interfere, so the protocol makes each new path prove it belongs to the same connection. That proof is a keyed hash computed with the secret the two hosts exchanged in the original handshake, and the secret is never sent across the network again.

items.desc: Join Connection: identifies the connection a new subflow joins.

items.desc: Data Sequence Signal: carries the mapping and the Data ACK.

items.label: ADD_ADDR
items.desc: Add Address: advertises another usable address.

items.label: REMOVE_ADDR
items.desc: Remove Address: withdraws an advertised address.

items.label: MP_PRIO
items.desc: Change Subflow Priority: marks a subflow as regular or backup.

items.label: MP_FAIL
items.desc: Fallback: signals a fall back to regular TCP.

items.label: MP_FASTCLOSE
items.desc: Fast Close: closes the whole MPTCP connection.

items.label: MP_TCPRST
items.desc: Subflow Reset: gives the reason for a subflow reset.
